---
title: "Silent Sunday"
author: "DK"
date: "2026-07-03"
categories: [observance]
---

My brother-in-law recently mentioned that a local mall would finally begin opening on Sundays starting this week.

The news came as a surprise—mostly because I had assumed it was already open.

Since I don't visit the area regularly, especially on weekends, I hadn't realized it was one of the few remaining places that is still closed on Sundays.

The news brought back memories of when I first arrived in this valley forty years ago.

Back then, virtually no businesses were open on Sundays.

The streets were quiet, and families dressed in their Sunday best can be seen walking to church.

Furthermore, it reminded me of an earlier time, when my family first arrived in the United States in the 1970s.

Our local town in Maryland had a few stores open, but even there, the pace was notably slower, and one could notice it was a day set aside for rest and worship.

![](images/20250525_231033_edit_1748184579305_edit_1748185047873 Copy.jpeg)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Historically, the day of rest was shaped by *blue laws*—regulations that restricted commerce, public entertainment, and unnecessary labor on Sundays.

Originating in colonial America to enforce Christian worship, these laws eventually helped turn Sunday into a broader social institution: a shared day when public activity naturally slowed down.

The enduring nature of these regulations was affirmed by the U.S. Supreme Court in *McGowan v. Maryland* (1961). In an 8–1 ruling, the Court held that Maryland’s Sunday closing laws did not violate the Establishment Clause, ("Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion”).[^1]

[^1]: https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/366/420/

The Justices reasoned that while blue laws originally had religious roots, their modern purpose had become secular—providing a uniform, statewide day of rest, health, and recreation for all citizens.

Fast forward fifty years, the vast majority of businesses now operate seven days a week to provide a uniform level of convenience, with only a few notable exceptions.

There are trade-offs when there are no distinctions in the days of the week.

In the pursuit of perpetual convenience, we have built a world of instant availability, but at the cost of asking more people to give up a shared day of rest.

Beyond restrictions and closures, a day of rest is necessary so that we can gather and nurture one another and rekindle that common bond that defines us as a community and a humanity.


![](images/20260801_071831~2.jpg)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

In 1 Samuel 8:20, the Israelites expressed a desire:

> *"That we also may be like all the nations; and that our king may judge us, and go out before us, and fight our battles."*

It has taken time, and the changes were subtle, but in our push for modern efficiency, we have, in essence, become like all the nations.

The quiet Sundays of the past may be largely gone, but preserving that pause is more than a nostalgia—it is an invitation for each of us to reflect on the early days of this nation, a country established like no other, and the wisdom behind those early blue laws.

In doing so, we come to recognize this truth:

> **the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.**[^2]

[^2]: **Mark 2:27**

Reclaiming that day of rest is receiving and exercising a gift designed to restore our souls and strengthen our society and humanity.
